items.prompt: A single-tenant deployment and a multi-tenant deployment both serve the same product. What's the defining difference?
choices: Multi-tenant systems don't use a database
Multi-tenant systems run one shared application/infrastructure serving many customers, each needing isolation from the others
Single-tenant systems can only ever have one user total
Multi-tenant systems are always slower than single-tenant ones
items.explanation: A tenant is a customer (or customer org) whose data and usage must stay separate from every other tenant's, even though the underlying application and infrastructure are shared. Single-tenant means one deployment per customer; multi-tenant means many customers share infrastructure, with isolation enforced by the software itself.
items.reference:
Single-tenant

one deployment per customer

Multi-tenant

shared infra, software enforces the boundary

Why: a tenant is defined by needing isolation, not by having its own hardware.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best definition of a 'tenant' in a multi-tenant system?
choices: A single database table
A customer or customer org whose data and usage must be kept separate from every other tenant's, on shared infrastructure
A synonym for 'user account'
A backup copy of the production database
items.explanation: A tenant is defined by the isolation requirement, not by any particular technical artifact — one tenant can have many user accounts, and the isolation boundary is between tenants, not between individual users within one.
items.reference:
Single-tenant

one deployment per customer

Multi-tenant

shared infra, software enforces the boundary

Why: a tenant is defined by needing isolation, not by having its own hardware.

items.prompt: A vendor advertises their product as 'multi-tenant SaaS.' What does that claim actually promise about the architecture?
choices: Every customer gets a fully separate deployment
Customers share the underlying application/infrastructure, with isolation enforced by the software itself
The product has no concept of separate customers at all
Customer data is never stored in a database
items.explanation: Multi-tenant specifically means shared infrastructure with software-enforced isolation between customers — the opposite of one dedicated deployment per customer, which is what 'single-tenant' would mean instead.
items.reference:
Single-tenant

one deployment per customer

Multi-tenant

shared infra, software enforces the boundary

Why: a tenant is defined by needing isolation, not by having its own hardware.

items.prompt: Which isolation model gives each tenant a completely separate database (or deployment), at the highest infrastructure cost?
choices: Silo
Pool
Bridge
None of these — all three share a database
items.explanation: Silo keeps tenants fully separate at the infrastructure level (separate database, sometimes a whole separate deployment), which maximizes isolation strength but also maximizes cost and onboarding time per tenant.
items.reference:
ModelSeparate
SiloDatabase / deployment
BridgeSchema / shard
PoolJust a tenant_id column

Why: the three models sit on a spectrum from full separation (silo) to full sharing (pool).

items.prompt: In the 'pool' isolation model, what actually keeps one tenant's rows separate from another's?
choices: A separate database per tenant
A tenant_id column plus enforcement in code or a database policy
Nothing — pool tenants share all data by design
A separate physical server per tenant
items.explanation: Pool shares everything — application, database, tables — down to individual rows. The only thing separating tenants is a tenant_id column and whatever actually enforces filtering by it, whether that's application code or a database policy like row-level security.
items.reference:
ModelSeparate
SiloDatabase / deployment
BridgeSchema / shard
PoolJust a tenant_id column

Why: the three models sit on a spectrum from full separation (silo) to full sharing (pool).

items.prompt: The 'bridge' model is often chosen as a middle ground between silo and pool. What does it typically share, and what does it keep separate?
choices: Shares nothing, separates everything (same as silo)
Shares the app and database server, keeps a schema or shard separate per tenant
Shares database rows, separates nothing
Shares nothing but the UI theme
items.explanation: Bridge runs shared application and database infrastructure — like pool — but gives each tenant its own schema or shard within that shared server, which is more isolation than a bare tenant_id column without the full cost of a dedicated database per tenant.
items.reference:
ModelSeparate
SiloDatabase / deployment
BridgeSchema / shard
PoolJust a tenant_id column

Why: the three models sit on a spectrum from full separation (silo) to full sharing (pool).

items.prompt: A query against a shared 'orders' table returns another tenant's orders. What's the most likely direct cause, under the pool isolation model?
choices: The database ran out of disk space
The query was missing a tenant_id filter
The tenant connected over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS
The load balancer routed the request to the wrong data center
items.explanation: Under pool, tenant rows live in the same tables — the only thing separating them is the tenant_id filter. A query that omits it will happily return every tenant's rows, because nothing else in the shared schema stops it.
items.reference:
🔓 Missing filter — the query runs fine, just against the wrong scope

Why: in the pool model, the tenant filter is the entire isolation boundary — there's no infra-level backstop.

items.prompt: Why is a missing tenant_id filter especially dangerous specifically under the pool isolation model?
choices: Because pool has no separate infra boundary to fall back on — the filter is the only thing keeping tenants apart
Because pool always encrypts data with the wrong key
Because pool doesn't support SQL databases
Because pool requires a VPN per tenant
items.explanation: Under silo or bridge, even a badly written query is still bounded by a database or schema that only contains one tenant's data. Under pool, there is no such backstop — the tenant_id filter is the entire isolation mechanism, so a missing filter is a direct, unguarded leak.
items.reference:
🔓 Missing filter — the query runs fine, just against the wrong scope

Why: in the pool model, the tenant filter is the entire isolation boundary — there's no infra-level backstop.

items.prompt: One tenant's huge nightly export makes every other tenant's dashboard slow, even though no data was leaked to anyone. What is this called?
choices: A data leak
A noisy neighbor
A cold start
A cache invalidation bug
items.explanation: Noisy neighbor describes exactly this: a tenant's usage pattern degrading shared infrastructure for everyone else on it, with no data crossing any boundary — it's a load isolation failure, not a data isolation failure.
items.reference:
Data leak

wrong rows returned

Noisy neighbor

everyone gets slower, no rows leak

Why: noisy neighbor is a load problem, not a data problem — the two need different fixes.

items.prompt: Which mechanism specifically addresses a 'noisy neighbor' problem?
choices: Row-level security
A per-tenant limit on shared resource usage
A stronger password policy
A CDN in front of static assets
items.explanation: Row-level security governs which rows a tenant can see, not how much of the shared database's capacity they can consume. Capping usage per tenant — a rate limit or resource quota — is what actually stops one tenant from starving the others.
items.reference:
Data leak

wrong rows returned

Noisy neighbor

everyone gets slower, no rows leak

Why: noisy neighbor is a load problem, not a data problem — the two need different fixes.

items.prompt: A tenant's data is perfectly isolated by row-level security, but their queries still slow down other tenants. What kind of isolation failure is this?
choices: A data isolation failure
A load/resource isolation failure
An authentication failure
An encryption failure
items.explanation: Data isolation and load isolation are separate guarantees. Correct row-level security fully solves data isolation but says nothing about CPU, I/O, or connection usage — a resource isolation failure requires a resource-level fix.
items.reference:
Data leak

wrong rows returned

Noisy neighbor

everyone gets slower, no rows leak

Why: noisy neighbor is a load problem, not a data problem — the two need different fixes.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a trustworthy way to determine which tenant a request belongs to?
choices: A verified JWT claim
A subdomain resolved by the router
A client-supplied header that nobody validates
A path prefix resolved by the router
items.explanation: An unverified, client-supplied header is just a claim the client typed — nothing stops a client from setting X-Tenant-Id to any value it wants. A verified token, a router-resolved subdomain, or a router-resolved path prefix all come from a source the system controls or has already checked.
items.reference:
SignalTrustworthy?
Verified JWT claimYes
Router-resolved subdomain/pathYes
Unvalidated client headerNo

Why: identity has to come from something the system verified, not something the client simply asserted.

items.prompt: Why must tenant identity be resolved from a verified source (like a checked JWT) rather than a raw client-supplied value?
choices: Because verification is a TCP-level requirement
Because an unverified value is just a claim the client could set to any tenant it wants
Because JWTs are the only valid transport for HTTP
Because raw values are always too short to be useful
items.explanation: If tenant identity is taken from something the client controls without verification, a malicious or buggy client can simply claim to be a different tenant — the 'identification' provides no actual guarantee, defeating the point of isolation.
items.reference:
SignalTrustworthy?
Verified JWT claimYes
Router-resolved subdomain/pathYes
Unvalidated client headerNo

Why: identity has to come from something the system verified, not something the client simply asserted.

items.prompt: In the shared-schema pattern, what single column is most commonly relied on to separate tenants' rows within the same table?
choices: created_at
tenant_id
id
updated_by
items.explanation: The tenant_id column is the row-level marker that says which tenant a given row belongs to — every read and write against a shared table has to key off of it for isolation to hold.
items.reference:
orders(id, tenant_id, amount)

Why: tenant_id is the row-level marker every filter and policy keys off of.

items.prompt: What's the core risk of relying purely on 'every developer remembers to filter by tenant_id' as the only enforcement mechanism?
choices: It's computationally too slow to check
A query added later, under time pressure, can forget the filter and nothing stops it from running
SQL doesn't support WHERE clauses on non-primary-key columns
It only works with NoSQL databases
items.explanation: Convention-based enforcement depends on every developer remembering the rule on every query, forever, including six months from now under deadline pressure. Nothing in the system itself catches the mistake before it ships.
items.reference:
orders(id, tenant_id, amount)

Why: tenant_id is the row-level marker every filter and policy keys off of.

items.prompt: A team adds a new report query against a shared table. What's the risky assumption if the tenant filter is enforced only by convention, not tooling?
choices: That the report query will run too slowly
That every future author of every future query will remember to add the filter, under all conditions, forever
That the database can't physically store more rows
That tenant_id values can't be indexed
items.explanation: The risk isn't about this one query — it's that the safety of every tenant's data now depends on an unenforced human habit holding across every future change to the codebase, which is exactly the assumption that broke in L1's Incident 1.
items.reference:
orders(id, tenant_id, amount)

Why: tenant_id is the row-level marker every filter and policy keys off of.

items.prompt: What does enabling row-level security (RLS) in Postgres change about how the database answers queries?
choices: It encrypts the entire database file at rest
It filters rows according to a policy, even if the query itself has no WHERE clause for it
It disables all write operations
It compresses the table on disk
items.explanation: RLS applies a policy at the database level that filters rows regardless of what the query text says — even a query that forgets to filter by tenant still only gets rows the policy allows through.
items.reference:
🛡️ RLS policy — checked by the database on every query, not by the query text itself

Why: RLS moves the tenant guarantee from the query author's memory into the database engine.

items.prompt: In L2's RLS policy example, what does the policy check against to decide which rows a query can see?
choices: The raw SQL text of the query
A session variable set for the current connection (current_setting)
The client's IP address
The table's total row count
items.explanation: The policy in L2's example checks tenant_id against current_setting('app.current_tenant') — a value the application sets on the database session, not something derived from parsing the query text.
items.reference:
🛡️ RLS policy — checked by the database on every query, not by the query text itself

Why: RLS moves the tenant guarantee from the query author's memory into the database engine.

items.prompt: Why does moving tenant isolation from application code into a row-level security policy make the guarantee stronger?
choices: Because RLS makes every query run faster
Because it no longer depends on every developer remembering to add a filter at every query site — the database enforces it uniformly
Because RLS removes the need for a tenant_id column entirely
Because RLS lets the database run without any connections
items.explanation: RLS turns a convention ('always filter by tenant_id') into something checked automatically on every single query by the database itself — the same enforcement L2 contrasted as 'a convention vs. an enforced boundary.'
items.reference:
🛡️ RLS policy — checked by the database on every query, not by the query text itself

Why: RLS moves the tenant guarantee from the query author's memory into the database engine.

items.prompt: Compared to pool, why does the silo model typically cost more per tenant?
choices: Because silo tenants get fewer features
Because each tenant gets dedicated infrastructure instead of sharing it with others
Because silo requires more application code to be written
Because silo always uses a slower database engine
items.explanation: Dedicated infrastructure per tenant means no economies of scale across tenants — the cost that pool amortizes across many tenants sharing one database, silo pays per tenant individually.
items.reference:
ModelCost per tenant
SiloHighest
BridgeMedium
PoolLowest

Why: sharing infrastructure across tenants is what makes pool cheaper per tenant.

items.prompt: Onboarding a new tenant is typically fastest under which isolation model, and why?
choices: Silo, because dedicated infrastructure provisions instantly
Pool, because a new tenant is often just a new row/tenant_id rather than new infrastructure
Bridge, because new schemas require zero setup
They're all equally fast regardless of model
items.explanation: Under pool, onboarding a tenant usually means inserting a tenant record and its rows into already-running shared infrastructure — no new database, server, or schema to provision, which is what makes it the fastest to onboard.
items.reference:
ModelCost per tenant
SiloHighest
BridgeMedium
PoolLowest

Why: sharing infrastructure across tenants is what makes pool cheaper per tenant.

items.prompt: Why does a per-tenant rate limit need to be keyed by tenant_id, rather than being one global limit for the whole system?
choices: A global limit lets any single tenant consume the entire shared capacity, defeating the point of isolating tenants from each other's load
Global limits are not supported by any web framework
Per-tenant limits are always cheaper to compute than global ones
It makes no practical difference either way
items.explanation: A shared, global limit is exactly the noisy-neighbor problem restated — one tenant can still consume the entire allowance, starving everyone else. Only a limit tracked independently per tenant guarantees one tenant's usage can't reduce what another has available.
items.reference:
Global limit

one tenant can exhaust it all

Per-tenant limit

independent allowance each

Why: only an independent-per-tenant limit stops one tenant's usage from affecting another's.

items.prompt: A system enforces row-level security perfectly but has no per-tenant rate limiting. Which L1 incident is it still exposed to?
choices: The data leak
The noisy neighbor
Neither incident
Both incidents equally
items.explanation: Row-level security fully addresses data isolation (Incident 1), but does nothing to cap shared resource consumption — a tenant can still degrade shared infrastructure for everyone else, which is exactly Incident 2, the noisy neighbor.
items.reference:
Global limit

one tenant can exhaust it all

Per-tenant limit

independent allowance each

Why: only an independent-per-tenant limit stops one tenant's usage from affecting another's.

items.prompt: What does a per-tenant rate limit directly protect against?
choices: SQL injection attacks
One tenant's request volume degrading shared resources for other tenants
Expired TLS certificates
Malformed JSON request bodies
items.explanation: A rate limit caps how much of a shared resource (requests per second, connections, CPU time) one tenant can consume, which is precisely what stops a single tenant's spike from becoming everyone else's outage.
items.reference:
Global limit

one tenant can exhaust it all

Per-tenant limit

independent allowance each

Why: only an independent-per-tenant limit stops one tenant's usage from affecting another's.

items.prompt: Per L2's sequence diagram, at what point should tenant identity ideally be resolved and trusted?
choices: At the very end, right before the response is sent
As early as possible (e.g. gateway/middleware), then carried forward as context
Only inside the database layer, never earlier
It should be re-derived independently at every layer
items.explanation: Resolving tenant identity once, early, and passing it forward as trusted context avoids re-deriving it from something a client could tamper with at every downstream layer — each unnecessary re-derivation is another chance to get it wrong.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Resolve once, early (gateway/middleware)
2️⃣ Carry forward as trusted context
3️⃣ Every layer reuses it, never re-derives it

Why: re-deriving identity at every layer multiplies the chances of trusting the wrong source.

items.prompt: Why is re-deriving tenant identity independently at every layer, instead of carrying trusted context forward, a risk?
choices: It's simply slower to write the code that way
Each independent derivation is a chance to read from an untrusted source or get it wrong, multiplying the surface for a mistake
It uses noticeably more disk space
It's incompatible with HTTPS
items.explanation: If every layer independently pulls tenant identity from wherever is convenient (a body field, a query param), one careless layer can end up trusting an unverified value — the risk grows with every extra place identity gets re-derived instead of passed forward.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Resolve once, early (gateway/middleware)
2️⃣ Carry forward as trusted context
3️⃣ Every layer reuses it, never re-derives it

Why: re-deriving identity at every layer multiplies the chances of trusting the wrong source.

items.prompt: Write scopeRows(rows, tenantId) so it returns only the rows whose tenantId field matches the given tenantId — the same enforcement TenantScopedQuery.find() relies on above.

tests.description: returns only the matching tenant's rows
tests.expr: expect(scopeRows([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'acme' }, { id: 2, tenantId: 'globex' }], 'acme')).toEqual([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'acme' }])

tests.description: returns an empty array when no rows match
an empty input returns an empty array

items.explanation: A plain .filter() against tenantId is the minimal version of what TenantScopedQuery does in its constructor — the important property isn't the filter itself (that's one line) but that it's the *only* path to reading rows, so there's no call site that can skip it.
items.reference:
🔒 scopeRows — the single, unavoidable filter point for every read

Why: making the filter the only way to read data is what turns a convention into an enforced boundary.

items.prompt: Write scopeTickets(tickets, tenantId) that returns only the support tickets belonging to tenantId, preserving their original relative order.

tests.description: keeps only the matching tenant's tickets, in order
tests.expr: expect(scopeTickets([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'a' }, { id: 2, tenantId: 'b' }, { id: 3, tenantId: 'a' }], 'a')).toEqual([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'a' }, { id: 3, tenantId: 'a' }])

tests.description: returns an empty array for a tenant with no tickets

items.explanation: .filter() naturally preserves the original order of the elements it keeps, so no extra sorting is needed — the same simple filter is the core of enforcing tenant scope, whatever the row's shape or the table's name.
items.reference:
🔒 scopeRows — the single, unavoidable filter point for every read

Why: making the filter the only way to read data is what turns a convention into an enforced boundary.

items.prompt: Write scopeDocuments(docs, tenantId) that throws an Error if tenantId is falsy, and otherwise returns only docs belonging to that tenant — mirroring the constructor guard TenantScopedQuery uses above.

tests.description: throws when tenantId is undefined
throws when tenantId is an empty string
returns matching docs when tenantId is valid

items.explanation: Throwing on a missing tenantId turns 'forgot to pass a tenant' from a silent bug (which could otherwise return everything, or nothing, depending on how the filter is written) into an immediate, loud failure at the exact call site that made the mistake.
items.reference:
🔒 scopeRows — the single, unavoidable filter point for every read

Why: making the filter the only way to read data is what turns a convention into an enforced boundary.

items.prompt: Simulate a Postgres row-level-security policy: write applyRls(allRows, sessionTenantId) that returns only the rows satisfying tenant_id = sessionTenantId — as if the database applied this filter no matter what the original query looked like.

tests.description: filters to only the session's tenant
tests.expr: expect(applyRls([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'acme' }, { id: 2, tenantId: 'globex' }], 'acme')).toEqual([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'acme' }])

tests.description: a session for a tenant with no rows gets an empty result, not another tenant's rows

items.explanation: This mirrors what a real RLS policy does at the database level: it filters the full row set by the session's tenant identity regardless of the query's own WHERE clause — the policy runs on top of, not instead of, whatever the query already asked for.
items.reference:
🛡️ applyRls — filters as if the database itself enforced it, independent of the query text

Why: an RLS-style filter applies on top of every query, not only to queries that remembered to ask for it.

items.prompt: Simulate a row-level-security policy for a 'contracts' table: write applyContractsRls(allRows, sessionTenantId) that returns only the current session tenant's contracts, and never a mix of tenants even if allRows already contains several tenants interleaved.

tests.description: never returns a mix of tenants
tests.expr: expect(applyContractsRls([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'a' }, { id: 2, tenantId: 'b' }, { id: 3, tenantId: 'a' }], 'a')).toEqual([{ id: 1, tenantId: 'a' }, { id: 3, tenantId: 'a' }])

tests.description: an empty table returns an empty result

items.explanation: The policy has to hold for every row in the table, not just a curated subset — interleaved tenants in the raw data is exactly the situation RLS is meant for, since the underlying storage genuinely does mix tenants together.
items.reference:
🛡️ applyRls — filters as if the database itself enforced it, independent of the query text

Why: an RLS-style filter applies on top of every query, not only to queries that remembered to ask for it.

items.prompt: Write consume(bucket, nowMs) implementing one step of a token-bucket rate limiter, mirroring TenantRateLimiter.tryConsume above. bucket has { tokens, capacity, refillPerSecond, lastRefillMs }. Refill tokens based on elapsed time since lastRefillMs (capped at capacity), then consume one token if at least 1 is available. Return a new object spreading bucket, with updated tokens, lastRefillMs: nowMs, and an added allowed boolean.

tests.description: allows a request when tokens are available and no time has passed
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 2, capacity: 2, refillPerSecond: 1, lastRefillMs: 0 }; expect(consume(b, 0).allowed).toBe(true)

tests.description: rejects a request when the bucket is empty and no time has passed
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 2, refillPerSecond: 1, lastRefillMs: 0 }; expect(consume(b, 0).allowed).toBe(false)

tests.description: refills over elapsed time, then allows and consumes one token
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 5, refillPerSecond: 1, lastRefillMs: 0 }; const r = consume(b, 2000); expect(r.allowed).toBe(true); expect(r.tokens).toBe(1)

tests.description: refill is capped at capacity, never exceeding it
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 3, refillPerSecond: 10, lastRefillMs: 0 }; const r = consume(b, 10000); expect(r.tokens).toBe(2)

items.explanation: Refilling first (capped at capacity) and only then checking/consuming is what lets a bucket that's been idle for a while allow a burst again, while a bucket that's been busy stays limited to its steady refill rate — exactly the burst-then-throttle shape TenantRateLimiter needs for a tenant that occasionally spikes.
items.reference:
🪣 Refill, cap, then consume — in that order, every call

Why: refilling before checking is what lets an idle tenant burst again without being permanently penalized for a past spike.

items.prompt: Write consume(bucket, nowMs), the same token-bucket step as above: bucket has { tokens, capacity, refillPerSecond, lastRefillMs }. Refill (capped at capacity) based on elapsed time, consume one token if available, and return a new bucket object with an allowed boolean.

tests.description: a fresh, full bucket allows the first request
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 10, capacity: 10, refillPerSecond: 2, lastRefillMs: 0 }; expect(consume(b, 0).allowed).toBe(true)

tests.description: an exhausted bucket with zero elapsed time rejects the request
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 10, refillPerSecond: 2, lastRefillMs: 500 }; expect(consume(b, 500).allowed).toBe(false)

tests.description: one second of elapsed time refills exactly refillPerSecond tokens
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 10, refillPerSecond: 2, lastRefillMs: 0 }; const r = consume(b, 1000); expect(r.allowed).toBe(true); expect(r.tokens).toBe(1)

items.explanation: The elapsed-time-to-tokens conversion (elapsedSeconds * refillPerSecond) is what makes the limiter rate-based instead of just a fixed quota — a tenant idle for a while naturally regains capacity, without any separate reset step or scheduled job.
items.reference:
🪣 Refill, cap, then consume — in that order, every call

Why: refilling before checking is what lets an idle tenant burst again without being permanently penalized for a past spike.

items.prompt: Write consume(bucket, nowMs), the same token-bucket step as the earlier variants: bucket has { tokens, capacity, refillPerSecond, lastRefillMs }. Refill (capped at capacity) based on elapsed time, consume one token if available, and return a new bucket object with an allowed boolean.

tests.description: consuming repeatedly with no elapsed time eventually rejects
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 1, capacity: 1, refillPerSecond: 1, lastRefillMs: 0 }; const r1 = consume(b, 0); const r2 = consume(r1, 0); expect(r1.allowed).toBe(true); expect(r2.allowed).toBe(false)

tests.description: a very long idle period still only refills up to capacity, not beyond it
tests.expr: const b = { tokens: 0, capacity: 4, refillPerSecond: 1, lastRefillMs: 0 }; const r = consume(b, 100000); expect(r.tokens).toBe(3)

items.explanation: Capping refilled at bucket.capacity is what stops an idle tenant from banking an unlimited burst — no matter how long the bucket sits unused, it can never hold more than capacity tokens at once.
items.reference:
🪣 Refill, cap, then consume — in that order, every call

Why: refilling before checking is what lets an idle tenant burst again without being permanently penalized for a past spike.

items.prompt: Write hasCrossTenantLeak(rows, tenantId) that returns true if any row in rows belongs to a different tenant than tenantId — an automated assertion that would have caught Incident 1 before it reached production.

tests.description: no leak when every row matches the tenant
detects a leak when any row belongs to another tenant
an empty result set has no leak

items.explanation: .some() short-circuits on the first mismatch, which is exactly the right semantics for a leak check: a single wrong-tenant row is already a failure, there's no need to keep scanning once one is found.

🧪 hasCrossTenantLeak — an assertion an integration test can run on every endpoint's response

throws when at least one row belongs to another tenant

Why: a reusable leak-detection assertion is what turns 'this shouldn't happen' into something CI actually checks.

items.prompt: In the silo model, each tenant has its own database connection string. Write resolveConnection(connectionsByTenant, tenantId) that returns the right connection string, and throws an Error if the tenant has no configured connection — never silently falling back to another tenant's database.

tests.description: returns the correct connection string for a known tenant
throws for an unconfigured tenant rather than returning undefined

items.explanation: Throwing on an unknown tenant is deliberate: silently returning undefined (or worse, a default connection) risks a request being served against the wrong database, or none at all, without any signal that something was misconfigured.
items.reference:
🗺️ resolveConnection — unknown tenant fails loudly, never falls back silently

Why: in the silo model, resolving the wrong connection is as bad as a query-level cross-tenant leak.

items.prompt: In the silo model, each tenant is pinned to a specific shard host. Write resolveShardHost(shardsByTenant, tenantId, defaultShard) that returns the tenant's assigned shard if configured, and otherwise returns defaultShard — but only when tenantId itself is a known key of an unrelated allow-list; for this exercise, just return shardsByTenant[tenantId] if present, else defaultShard (no allow-list needed).

tests.description: returns the tenant's assigned shard when configured
falls back to defaultShard for an unconfigured tenant

items.explanation: A default shard is a reasonable fallback for a bridge/pool-style shared shard, in contrast to resolveConnection's silo case above — the right failure behavior (throw vs. fall back to a real, safe default) depends on whether an unconfigured tenant is an error condition or a normal 'goes to the shared pool' case.
